question: Is there a relationship between rheumatoid arthritis and periodontal disease?
answer: Yes, in 1,412 individuals attending the University of Queensland's School of Dentistry, the prevalence of self-reported rheumatoid arthritis was significantly higher in patients referred for periodontal treatment (3.95%) than in those not referred (0.66%) or the general population (1%) [PMID:10783841]. Among referred patients with rheumatoid arthritis, 62.5% had advanced forms of periodontal disease [PMID:10783841]. These findings support a relationship between rheumatoid arthritis and periodontal disease, though the study design based on self-report and dental records does not establish causality [PMID:10783841].

question: Can medical students contribute to quality assurance programmes in day surgery?
answer: Yes, senior medical students contributed to quality assurance in day surgery in a study where 59 final-year students followed 621 cases, representing 14.1% of day surgery cases [PMID:10354335]. answer: The supplied passages do not settle whether minilaparoscopic inguinal hernia repair is feasible; they only report that an initial experience of minilaparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (miniTAPP) repair of groin hernia defects was performed at two institutions using instruments 5 mm or less in diameter, without providing outcomes or feasibility data [PMID:15954832]. Other supplied studies concern laparoscopic repair of incarcerated abdominal hernias (2688 laparoscopic vs 15,562 open) [PMID:26541733], day-case elective inguinal hernia repair in elderly patients [PMID:25159543], and pediatric laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair [PMID:17362187][PMID:22870947], but none address minilaparoscopic inguinal hernia repair feasibility.

chunks.text: There is a paucity of literature surrounding the safety and feasibility of laparoscopic repair for acutely incarcerated abdominal hernias. The objective of this study was to compare the 30-day morbidity and mortality between laparoscopic and open repairs of incarcerated abdominal hernias.

A retrospective cohort study was conducted using data from the National Surgery Quality Improvement Program from 2005 to 2012. The study population was selected using ICD-9 diagnostic codes describing abdominal hernias with obstruction, but without gangrene. Cases with documented bowel resection were excluded. However, there was no statistical difference with respect to the 30-day reoperation (OR 0.81, p = 0.28, 95 % CI 0.56-1.18) or mortality rates (OR 0.94, p = 0.80, 95 % CI 0.58-1.53).

The aim of this paper is to illustrate retrospectively the results of an initial experience of minilaparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal (miniTAPP) repair of groin hernia defects performed at two institutions.

Sixteen male infants with large inguinal hernias (hernia extending to the bottom of the scrotum and the diameter of the open internal ring>2 cm on laparoscopy) underwent laparoscopic hernia repair. An open internal ring was considered an indication for hernia repair. The needle, carrying 3-0 nylon nonabsorbable sutures, was introduced through the groin skin at the internal inguinal ring and the internal ring was closed by taking continuous sutures to approximate the edges of the ring. The needle was then taken out through the entry point and the knot was tied extracorporeally and buried in the subcutaneous tissue. question: Women with synchronous primary cancers of the endometrium and ovary: do they have Lynch syndrome?
answer: In a series of 59 women with synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancers who had tumor blocks analyzed, 7 had evidence of Lynch syndrome: 2 met Amsterdam criteria and 5 additional medium-risk patients had molecular findings consistent with a germline MSH2 or MLH1 mutation, while no low-risk patients had such findings [PMID:16361634]. Thus, some women with synchronous endometrial and ovarian cancers do have Lynch syndrome, but in this study it was confined to those with high- or medium-risk family histories [PMID:16361634].

chunks.text: Lynch syndrome (hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer; HNPCC) is an autosomal-dominant cancer predisposition syndrome that increases risk for multiple cancers, including colon, endometrial, and ovarian cancer. question: Does rural or urban residence make a difference to neonatal outcome in premature birth?
answer: Rural residence was associated with worse neonatal outcome among very premature infants. question: Counter sampling combined with medical provider education: do they alter prescribing behavior?
answer: In a pretest-post-test controlled study in two rural southeastern Idaho clinics, pharmacists' education plus counter samples significantly reduced COX-2 NSAID prescribing among 8 intervention providers from 38.9% to 23.7% of total NSAID prescriptions (P<0.05), while 7 control providers had a non-significant decrease from 67.5% to 62% [PMID:17076590]. However, the same intervention did not stop significant increases in focus nonsedating antihistamines (86.7% to 93.1%, P<0.05) and proton pump inhibitors (68.9% to 86.2%, P<0.05) [PMID:17076590]. question: Recurrent spontaneous abortion and skewed X-inactivation: is there an association?
answer: In a study of 357 women with recurrent spontaneous abortion (2 or more losses), the rate of extreme skewed X-inactivation (90% or greater) was 8.6%, which was not statistically different from the infertility, spontaneous abortion, or multiparous groups [PMID:17403428]. question: Is tumour expression of VEGF associated with venous invasion and survival in pT3 renal cell carcinoma?
answer: In 78 patients with pT3a/pT3b renal cell carcinoma grouped by renal vein or vena cava invasion, VEGF expression was not significantly different among the groups; only tumour size differed significantly [PMID:17489316]. question: Cholestasis associated with small bowel atresia: do we always need to investigate?
answer: Among 55 patients with small bowel atresia (SBA) reviewed retrospectively, 24 of 53 (45%) developed postoperative cholestasis, but no patient had biliary atresia, no deaths were related to isolated cholestasis/cirrhosis, and cholestasis resolved spontaneously in all survivors [PMID:17502203]. Ten patients (36%) underwent in-depth evaluations and 8 (28%) had liver biopsy, suggesting these investigations may be unnecessary in many cases [PMID:17502203]. The study indicates that routine intensive or invasive investigation for cholestasis in SBA is not always required, though it is a single retrospective series and does not prove that investigation can be omitted in every case [PMID:17502203].

chunks.text: Cholestasis occurs frequently in patients with small bowel atresia (SBA) and is often attributed to prolonged parental nutrition. question: Can you deliver accurate tidal volume by manual resuscitator?
answer: Accurate tidal volume delivery with a manual resuscitator is difficult and varies by squeezing technique and provider [PMID:18843057]. question: Is being small for gestational age a risk factor for retinopathy of prematurity?
answer: In a prospective cohort of preterm infants with birth weight ≤1,500 g and gestational age ≤32 weeks, any-stage ROP occurred in 24.7% of SGA infants versus 33.2% of AGA infants (p=0.111), and severe ROP in 6.2% versus 7.5% (p=0.779) [PMID:19198736]. question: Does telmisartan prevent hepatic fibrosis in rats with alloxan-induced diabetes?
answer: Telmisartan treatment in alloxan-induced diabetic rats (10 mg/kg/day orally for 30 days; 15 adult male rats across non-diabetic, diabetic control, and diabetic telmisartan groups) was associated with no hepatic TGF-beta immunoreactivity, whereas diabetic controls were strongly immunoreactive. answer: In a retrospective study of 1000 consecutive patients undergoing routine contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT (excluding multiphasic indications), delayed phase imaging provided added benefit in only 42 patients (4.2%), while it was of no benefit in 958 patients (95.8%) [PMID:24450673]. Most delayed-phase findings were incidental (e.g., liver hemangioma n=12, adrenal adenoma n=12, parapelvic renal cysts n=6) that could have been confirmed with noninvasive follow-up, and only one patient (0.1%) had a renal mass detected solely on delayed phase [PMID:24450673]. Delayed phase imaging increased effective radiation dose by a mean of 59.5% [PMID:24450673]. These findings suggest that for routine abdominopelvic CT, the additional radiation and time of delayed imaging are not justified given the very low yield [PMID:24450673].

question: Clinical identifiers for early-stage primary/idiopathic adhesive capsulitis: are we seeing the real picture?
answer: Among 64 patients diagnosed with early-stage adhesive capsulitis by a physical therapist or medical practitioner, only 16 (25%) had a positive anesthetic response, defined as ≥70% pain relief for passive external rotation after intra-articular corticosteroid and local anesthetic [PMID:24652474]. Of the 8 proposed clinical identifiers, univariate logistic regression linked global loss of passive range of movement (OR=0.26, P=.03), pain at the end of range of all measured active movements (OR=0.06, P=.02), and global loss of passive glenohumeral movements (OR=0.23, P=.02) to a positive anesthetic response, but after stepwise removal, pain at the end of range of all measured active movements remained the only identifier and was associated with reduced odds of a positive response [PMID:24652474]. These findings suggest the clinical picture may be misleading because most clinically diagnosed early-stage cases did not meet the anesthetic reference standard, and no recognized reference standard exists for diagnosing early-stage adhesive capsulitis [PMID:24652474]. The diagnoses were also clinician based [PMID:15546647].

The lack of a recognized reference standard for diagnosing early-stage adhesive capsulitis remains problematic in all related research.

question: Pharmacologic regimens for knee osteoarthritis prevention: can they be cost-effective?
answer: Pharmacologic prophylaxis for knee osteoarthritis can be cost-effective only in selected high-risk patients and at lower drug prices, not across all risk groups [PMID:24487044]. In the high-risk cohort (obese with a history of knee injury), base-case DMOAD prophylaxis versus standard care increased QALYs by 0.04 and lifetime costs by $4,600, yielding an ICER of $118,000 per QALY gained [PMID:24487044]. ICERs exceeded $150,000/QALY in the knee-injury-only cohort, and the base-case DMOAD was less cost-effective than standard care in obese-only and no-risk-factor cohorts; regimens priced at $3,000 per year or higher had ICERs above US cost-effectiveness thresholds [PMID:24487044]. The other supplied passages concern total knee replacement use and decision aids, not pharmacologic prevention, so they do not address this question [PMID:27075333][PMID:15911724].

question: Are there risk factors that increase the rate of staple line leakage in patients undergoing primary sleeve gastrectomy for morbid obesity?

question: Do emergency ultrasound fellowship programs impact emergency medicine residents' ultrasound education?
answer: Emergency ultrasound (EUS) fellowship programs do appear to impact emergency medicine (EM) residents' ultrasound education, based on a cross-sectional study of 244 EM residents at 9 academic medical centers [PMID:24866606]. question: Is resected stomach volume related to weight loss after laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy?
answer: In a prospective study of 100 patients undergoing laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy, patients were divided into three groups by resected stomach volume (700–1,200 mL, n=21; 1,200–1,700 mL, n=62; >1,700 mL, n=17) [PMID:24827404]. question: Should early extubation be the goal for children after congenital cardiac surgery?
answer: The evidence supports early extubation as a goal when feasible for children after congenital cardiac surgery, including neonates [PMID:25156467]. question: Maternal creatine homeostasis is altered during gestation in the spiny mouse: is this a metabolic adaptation to pregnancy?
answer: In pregnant spiny mice (n=8) compared with age-matched virgin females (n=6), plasma creatine and renal creatine excretion decreased significantly from mid to late gestation (P<0.001 and P<0.05, respectively), and pregnancy increased lean tissue, kidney, liver, and heart mass at term [PMID:25885219]. question: Does hippocampal atrophy on MRI predict cognitive decline?
answer: In a prospective 2-year follow-up of 5 controls with hippocampal atrophy (HCA) and 5 without, 7 depressed subjects with HCA and 7 without, and 12 Alzheimer's disease patients with HCA and 12 without, there were no significant differences in rate of cognitive decline, mortality, or progression to dementia between those with and without HCA [PMID:9444542]. Another study found that Alzheimer's disease patients had greater bilateral hippocampal atrophy than controls, and right hippocampal size accounted for a significant portion of variance in cognitive scores independently of brain activity measures, but this was not a longitudinal decline analysis [PMID:12531952]. A separate prospective cohort measured annual hippocampal atrophy in 54 donepezil-treated and 93 untreated Alzheimer's disease patients over 1 year but reported only method and baseline comparability, not cognitive decline outcomes [PMID:15800138]. Thus, the supplied passages do not show that hippocampal atrophy on MRI predicts cognitive decline; the only relevant follow-up found no significant association [PMID:9444542].

question: Does lunar position influence the time of delivery?
answer: A retrospective analysis of 1248 spontaneous full-term deliveries over 36 lunar months found a connection between the distribution of deliveries and the lunar month [PMID:9550200]. The effect of lunar phases was particularly relevant in multiparae and plurigravidae, in whom the mean day of delivery corresponded to the first or second day after the full moon [PMID:9550200]. This indicates that lunar position can influence the time of delivery.

question: Does the Child Health Computing System adequately identify children with cerebral palsy?
answer: No, the Child Health Computing System did not adequately identify children with cerebral palsy in the one comparative study available [PMID:9602458]. In a Northern Ireland survey of children with cerebral palsy aged 5-9 years, 47% of the 135 cases on the Cerebral Palsy Register were not found on the Child Health Computing System, and most of those children had no computer record of any medical diagnosis [PMID:9602458]. Among the 82 children recorded on the Child Health Computing System, 12% were not on the Cerebral Palsy Register and 6% were found on follow-up not to have cerebral palsy, indicating both under-ascertainment and some false positives [PMID:9602458].
